articles.title: As extreme heat worsens, renters are gaining a ‘right to cooling’
articles.content:
Subjecting the incarcerated residents of Texas to extreme heat constitutes cruel and unusual punishment, and prisons statewide must install air conditioning by the end of 2029.

Although the ruling Judge Robert Pitman issued last month is unique in its invocation of the Constitution’s Eighth Amendment, it is an explicit recognition of an idea increasingly reflected in laws and policies nationwide: As extreme heat becomes more dangerous, even deadly, access to cooling is increasingly seen as a necessity rather than a luxury. This shift has been especially active in housing, where renters often face structural hurdles to accessing cool air, from high costs to explicit bans on the installation of air conditioning.

This summer, jurisdictions across the U.S. passed policies setting maximum indoor temperatures, requiring landlords to provide AC, or otherwise expanding tenants’ access to cooling. The state of Maryland, for instance, said property owners with 10 or more units must install AC if they renovate. In Spokane, Washington, where 14 people died during a heat wave in July, landlords must now provide “adequate cooling” in at least one room of each unit.

“You can no longer responsibly rent a place if you don’t have a way of keeping it cool, because people will die,” said Brian Henning, director of the Institute for Climate, Water, and the Environment at Gonzaga University and a leading advocate for the Spokane policy.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Indeed, a study from 2024 found that renters were three times more likely than homeowners to need medical attention due to heat exposure at home, and researchers estimate as many as 50,000 people died during the five heat waves Europe experienced this summer. But unlike the incarcerated in Texas, whose protection rests on the Eighth Amendment, renters’ claim to safe indoor temperatures rests on a different and less explicit legal foundation.

It’s based, in part, on the “implied warranty of habitability,” a legal principle requiring landlords to provide the basic necessities for life — things like running water — even when they aren’t explicitly guaranteed in a lease or by law. Heating has long been understood as part of that warranty. As extreme heat poses an increasing threat to health, advocates argue that protection from dangerously high indoor temperatures should be as well.

“You can’t run a place without heat,” said Doug Ruley, director of the Environmental Justice Clinic at the University of Miami School of Law. “The same is exactly true for cooling. I think the rights framing is powerful, and very consistent with how we Americans tend to think about things we care about.”

Tenants could, in theory, ask courts to recognize heat protection as part of the implied warranty of habitability. But rather than rely on judges, advocates have largely pursued explicit protections through housing codes and landlord-tenant laws.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Exactly what those protections should guarantee — and how they are implemented — is far from settled.

A Los Angeles woman attempts to keep her infant daughter cool during the heat wave that hit Southern California in September. The apartment she shares with her parents and brother does not have air conditioning. Jason Armond / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images

The first question is whether they should require air conditioning, as the ruling in Texas does, or simply establish a maximum allowable indoor temperature that property owners can comply with however they see fit. Clinton Andrews, director of the Center for Urban Policy Research at Rutgers University, believes the latter approach could encourage passive, energy-efficient methods, like planting trees or installing window shades. A well-designed performance standard also makes clear exactly what landlords are expected to achieve. Unlike a law that simply requires them to install AC or provide “adequate cooling,” a temperature threshold gives tenants and regulators something concrete to measure against.

Such a standard still requires deciding how hot is too hot, and there’s no universally accepted science on this. Some jurisdictions have settled on 82 degrees Fahrenheit. Others, like several cities in Canada, are exploring a limit closer to 79 degrees F. Stefano Schiavon, a professor of architecture and civil and environmental engineering at the University of California Berkeley, said this is to some extent influenced by physiology and culture because people regularly exposed to high temperatures can more readily adapt to hotter weather.

The same flexibility that appeals to Andrews, however, can also be a liability. Some housing advocates worry that a performance standard could allow a landlord to avoid providing the most effective — and costly — means of cooling: air conditioning.

“The only intervention that is going to protect people’s lives in a heat event is AC,” said Chelsea Kirk, advocacy and policy director for the south-L.A. nonprofit Strategic Actions for a Just Economy. During a major heat wave, she added, “tree shade is not gonna get us there.”

Jurisdictions are already experimenting with different approaches. Houston’s right-to-cooling ordinance, approved in August, requires AC. It establishes air conditioning as a health and safety standard for all rental housing, closing a loophole that had allowed landlords to forgo it in apartments with window screens. Spokane, Washington, stops short of requiring AC, but says landlords must reimburse their tenants up to $500 if they want to install it themselves.

Los Angeles County has taken the performance-standard approach in its unincorporated communities. Beginning January 1, landlords must provide a “safe and code-complaint method” of maintaining a maximum indoor air temperature of 82 degrees F. The city of Los Angeles voted in February to explore a similar measure, though adoption has been delayed.

Other jurisdictions have adopted variations on these protections. Since 2020, Austin, Texas; New Orleans, and New York City have passed cooling requirements, while Washington and Oregon have barred landlords from prohibiting tenants from installing their own AC units. In Arizona, the attorney general’s aggressive interpretation of housing laws has established what amounts to a de facto statewide AC requirement.

Henning said he’s been in talks with advocacy groups and state legislators about taking Spokane’s right-to-cooling policy statewide, while lawmakers and officials elsewhere in the U.S. and Canada are weighing similar measures.

One hurdle advocates will likely continue to face is cost. Landlords argue cooling requirements will lead to higher rents, though researchers say there’s scant evidence to support that. Some tenant advocates and other experts worry greater reliance on AC could mean higher utility bills. Supporters of such mandates concede that is a significant concern, but not a reason to deprive people of AC.

“Tenants can make their own choices. I don’t think somebody’s going to be, like, ‘Well, I’d rather risk dying tonight because I don’t want to turn on the AC,” said Michele Thomas, director of policy and advocacy for the nonprofit Washington State Housing Alliance.

C.J. Gabbe, an associate professor of environmental studies and sciences at Santa Clara University, said one way to help cover cooling costs would be to expand the federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program. The Trump administration fired the federal staff that administered the program last year and has proposed eliminating it, but Congress continues funding it. This month, the administration released about $3.6 billion for the current fiscal year.

Experts Grist spoke with stressed that expanding access to cooling can’t be a substitute for addressing the climate change that is making it increasingly necessary. Ultimately, Henning said, governments must address the underlying causes of the crisis by stopping the burning of fossil fuels. “Otherwise, these problems will continue to outstrip our ability to address them,” he told Grist. “We can’t just AC the world.”

This has broad societal impact as it addresses health and safety for vulnerable populations nationwide through new laws and policies. The story provides detailed examples of legal rulings, policy changes, and ongoing advocacy efforts, showing substantive progress in protecting tenants from deadly heat exposure.
articles.personality_title: Renters gain legal rights to cooling as heat waves worsen
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Extreme heat is becoming more dangerous, especially for people who live in rental homes without air conditioning. In Texas, a court ruled that prisons must install AC by 2029 because heat can harm inmates. This idea is spreading to housing laws across the United States.

**What happened** – This summer, many U.S. cities and states passed new rules requiring landlords to provide cooling during hot weather. For example, Maryland says landlords must add AC when they renovate large buildings, and Spokane, Washington, now requires landlords to offer at least one cooled room per rental unit. These rules aim to protect renters from health risks caused by extreme heat.

**Impact** – Renters are more likely than homeowners to get sick from heat at home. Laws are starting to treat cooling as a basic need, similar to heating or running water. This helps protect vulnerable people who can’t easily install AC themselves. Some places require landlords to provide AC, while others set a maximum indoor temperature to keep homes safe. These new rules could save lives during heat waves.

**What's next step** – Advocates want more places to pass clear cooling laws. Some argue for requiring air conditioning, while others prefer flexible standards that encourage energy-saving solutions like shade trees. There is also talk about helping low-income renters pay for higher electricity bills. Meanwhile, experts say cooling rules won’t solve the problem alone—fighting climate change remains essential.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New laws are giving renters the right to stay cool indoors as extreme heat grows more dangerous, marking important progress in housing safety.

articles.title: Climate change rarely goes on trial. This one could be a landmark.
articles.content:
Climate change gets a rare day in court today when 15 Canadian youth will accuse the federal government of violating their constitutional rights by failing to adequately address the country’s role in global warming. Although thousands of similar cases have been filed across the globe, legal experts said this long-awaited case is arguably the most consequential to reach trial.

The lawsuit is the latest in a yearslong campaign by young people who are using the courts to force elected officials to mitigate climate change. Like similar cases in the United States, including the landmark Held v. Montana, the plaintiffs in La Rose v. His Majesty the King argue that the government has violated their constitutional rights by allowing the crisis to continue.

Set in Vancouver, the proceedings are slated to last five weeks, with the 15 plaintiffs expected to testify alongside climate scientists and other experts. “It’s the chance for the young people to tell their story,” said Kelly Matheson, deputy director for global strategy at Our Children’s Trust, the nonprofit behind this case and many similar efforts around the world.

The outcome, while not precedent-setting outside of Canada, could prove persuasive in other climate litigation or spur new cases. “We found that some of the positive decisions from some countries have been inspirational in other countries,” said Michael Gerrard, faculty director of the Columbia University’s Sabin Center for Climate Change Law. “This trial will be closely watched.”

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The case began in 2019, when the youth, six of whom identify as Indigenous, filed suit. They alleged, among other things, that by not doing enough to combat climate change, the government had violated Section 7 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which guarantees “the right to life, liberty, and security of the person.” They also argued that federal action breached their equality protections granted under Section 15 of the charter because, as young people, they will bear a disproportionate share of the impacts of the crisis.

The original lawsuit took aim at much of Canada’s approach to climate change. The plaintiffs argued that the government had allowed emissions to remain dangerously high, set targets that fell short of what scientists said was necessary to avoid the worst outcomes, repeatedly failed to meet those targets, and continued supporting the development and expansion of fossil fuels.

Although the government did not challenge the reality of climate change, its arguments included a claim that the accusations were overly broad and the lawsuit improperly asked the court to resolve a political matter. A federal judge agreed and dismissed the case without a trial in 2020. The plaintiffs appealed. In 2023, the Federal Court of Appeal upheld the dismissal of the Section 15 claim but allowed the Section 7 arguments to proceed if the plaintiffs more specifically detailed the government conduct that violated their protected rights.

The plaintiffs amended their complaint to focus on the Canadian Net-Zero Emissions Accountability Act of 2021, which commits the country to achieving the law’s objectives by 2050, and the 2030 emissions reduction plan adopted under that law. They argue that the efforts don’t go far enough to avoid violating their charter rights in the context of climate change and that the government committed to the net-zero law.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

“Increasingly, people across Canada and the world are seeing the direct impacts of climate change,” said Andrew Gage, a staff lawyer for West Coast Environment Law who has worked on this case alongside Our Children’s Trust. “The plaintiffs will have their day in court.”

The Canadian Department of Justice referred a request for comment to Environment and Climate Change Canada, which declined an interview request but provided a written statement to Grist. “Our commitment to net-zero by 2050 has not wavered, and we are implementing an ambitious climate agenda,” a spokesperson, Samantha Bayard, wrote in an email. “The Government of Canada respects the role of the courts, the right of Canadians to bring matters before the courts, and the important role that an independent judiciary plays in our democracy.”

All 15 youths, who were between the ages of 10 and 19 when the suit was filed, are expected to testify. They will be joined by expert witnesses in climate science, renewable energy, children’s health, and economics. Closing arguments are scheduled for February with a decision expected sometime in 2027, although an appeal could delay a resolution. Still, it is unusual for such a case to even be heard.

“Seldom has climate been put on trial,” said James May, an environmental law professor at Washburn University who isn’t involved in this case but has supported some of Our Children’s Trust’s past work. He estimated that more than 3,000 climate cases have been filed worldwide over the past few decades, but most never reached a courtroom. The Hawai’i state Department of Transportation, for example, settled a lawsuit filed by 13 young people and agreed to develop a plan to zero out emissions from the transportation sector by 2045. The landmark case Juliana v. the United States was dismissed after years of litigation, and the Supreme Court declined to consider it.

Held v. Montana was a rare exception. After a seven-day trial in 2023, a judge ruled that the state’s energy permitting policies violated the plaintiffs’ right to “a clean and healthful environment,” which is enshrined in the state constitution. The state Supreme Court upheld that decision in 2024.

A similar outcome in Vancouver could have implications in other British commonwealth countries and beyond, said Matheson. “These courts are looking to each other,” she said. “There is momentum building.”

But even if the plaintiffs don’t win, May considers the trial a victory even before it starts. “It could serve as a blueprint for how to do this elsewhere,” he said. “It has already succeeded.”
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a significant legal case where Canadian youth are suing the federal government for failing to adequately address climate change, arguing it violates their constitutional rights. This case has broad implications for climate justice and youth rights, potentially influencing other countries and advancing legal accountability for climate action. It is a focused, substantive story with meaningful societal impact.

articles.title: Mentoring a lab colleague? Share your ‘CV of failures’ with them
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 26 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03410-7Melanie Stefan became a ‘poster child of failure’ after writing an article about it. Now she urges senior colleagues to be more open about career setbacks.
articles.content:
Alena Vdovchenko 00:04

So I’m a chemist and experimental scientist, so I don’t need to search very hard for examples of day-to-day failure.

Stephen Webster 00:12

That’s Dr Alena Vdovchenko, a postdoctoral scientist at Imperial College London, talking in April this year at the Failure in Science conference.

Alena Vdovchenko 00:22

In the lab, simply most of the things don’t work the way you plan them.

So sometimes you carefully design the experiment. You run it for sometimes weeks, months. It depends.

Maybe days if you’re lucky.

But then when you analyze the results, you realize that okay, you didn’t account for factor A.

So then you have to go back.

You need to redesign the experiment, maybe read more literature, go back to the lab.

Stephen Webster 00:48

Alena was speaking at the session called A Taxonomy of Failure, where we heard early career researchers explaining how, in real life, (let’s put it like this), things often don’t go quite as planned.

Alena Vdovchenko 01:01

But overall, I think a lot of chemistry is trial and error. And during my PhD, we have that quote printed in our lab.

Theory is when you know everything but nothing works.

Practice is when everything works but no one knows why.

In our lab, theory and practice are combined.

Nothing works, and no one knows why.

I feel like it’s very funny, but also very uncomfortably true.

Stephen Webster 01:30

I’m Dr Stephen Webster, director of the Good Science Project at Imperial College London, a programme that examines what we like about research culture, and what we don’t.

And in episode two, we hear panelist Melanie Stefan, professor of physiology at Berlin Medical School, talk about failure and the lab.

Melanie Stefan 01:57

My first big experience of failure in science was when I was doing my masters in a developmental biology lab, and I really had a difficult time there.

I didn’t quite know how to troubleshoot experiments if they failed. I didn’t quite understand what I was doing. I think it was not the right place for me.

And the worst day was when my supervisor called me into his office and said, "Melanie, I think you should really look for jobs outside of science."

And that was devastating because I had been studying science for many years at the time. I saw myself as a scientist. I didn’t really have a Plan B.

So much of my identity was being a scientist and doing science.

Not just that I loved doing it, and I was really interested in it, but also I didn’t know what else I could do.

So this was really a devastating failure for me.

And I wrote an article about this in Nature. It’s also the only thing I have published in Nature.

Other journals exist, and since then I’ve kind of become the poster child of failure, kind of without intending it.

So at the Failure in Science conference at Imperial College, I talked about this article I wrote called A CV of Failures.

And the story of that is after my master’s degree, (which I ended up completing in the end), I did a PhD, and I had a very great time there.

I had a lot of fun. It was quite a successful time for me.

But then I was done with that, and I needed to apply for funding to go to the next stage of my career as a postdoc.

And it was really hard. It was really hard to find funding. And I was rejected from, a lot of my funding applications were rejected. I started doubting myself.

And I also thought that, "Oh my God, I’m the first person this has happenened to."

Because all the other scientists around me, obviously, or like the scientists who were like a bit further ahead they were further ahead because they were ultimately successful in securing a postdoc position.

And so all I saw around me was ultimately the successes.

So I felt like I was the only one who had ever failed. So that made it even worse, and so this gave me the idea of writing this article calling for a CV of failures.

So the idea would be that the successful people in science would actually open up about their failures that they had on their way, and how many jobs they didn’t get, how many positions they weren’t admitted to, how many grants they failed to receive, how many papers were rejected, things like that.

So that younger scientists like I was at the time could actually take heart and see that this is actually a normal part of the process and that they’re not alone.

So that was the idea. And since then, I’ve kind of become the poster child of failure a little bit.

A lot of friends tell me, "Oh, Melanie, I read something about failure. I was thinking of you."

I was like, "Thank you. That is so nice."

I think it’s generally really cool that there has been following up on this article a bigger discussion about failure in science that the conference was also part of.

I think that’s really lovely. And it’s really lovely to see people come together and talk about this concept.

Melanie Stefan 05:43

The conference is called Failure in Science, but I’d like to smuggle in engineering. I know Mary already mentioned engineering in the last session, and I’m an engineer, and I think engineering has a very well developed tradition of understanding and learning from failure.

Melanie Stefan 06:03

So I liked the the session that was called "A View from the Lab.

And it was especially nice to to hear from the more junior scientists about how they interacted with failure and how they experienced it.

But I also thought the moderator George Constantinides is one thing that really that I found really interesting about what he said was how he compared it to engineering.

George Constantinides 06:27

And I think if I were to summarize the very broad literature on failure in engineering, at least my understanding is: number one, there is no failure without uncertainty.

And number two, structured ways from learning from failure are essential.

And I think those are things that we can carry forward into many different aspects of our work.

In general, I would kind of summarize by saying, in my view, if we want people to fly high, then we have to make it easy and safe to fail well.

Melanie Stefan 07:02

And in engineering, you have to fail. Like, that’s how. You build something, you try a prototype and then it fails, and you learn from that.

You watch how exactly it failed, you analyze it, and then you build the next better version, and the next version, the next version.

And I think the point he was making, and I really agree with that, is that we should treat scientific careers in the same way, and that we need to give people spaces where it’s safe to try something and fail, and then to talk about it, and learn from it, and then do better the next time and try again.

And maybe fail in a different way, but then build something in the end that’s better. So I really like that engineering analogy.

So one thing that also came up in a lot of the discussions at the conference, and that I think is really important, is the question of who actually gets to talk about failure and who gets to fail.

So the reason why I’m invited to conferences like that is that ultimately I did finish my master’s degree, and ultimately I did become a scientist.

And this is why I get to talk about failure is in my scientific career is because ultimately I have succeeded.

And what about the people, though, who have failed?

And I use the word advisedly.

It’s not always like a personal failure.

But people who have set out to have a life in science and are now doing something else. We never hear from them, right, because they are not in that space anymore?

So I think it takes a certain amount of privilege and position to be allowed to talk about failure.

And also, when I was a young scientist and I was looking for positions, I was sometimes, like, googling my name, and then the first thing that came up was A CV of Failures.

And I thought that was really strategically not that clever of me.

But I was not in a position then where it was much less safe to open up about failures.

And now I’m in a position where I can do it because I have a professorship. Nothing is nothing bad is going to happen to me.

So this privilege of opening up about failure is really important.

And then also failure itself is something that you need quite a bit of privilege to do.

So for me, I was able to apply for several postdoc grants and failed to get them until there was finally one that I succeeded in getting.

I was in a position to do that because my institute was happy to pay me for another year after I finished my PhD, and my supervisor was happy to keep me around in the lab, and my visa status didn’t depend on me securing funding right away.

So, and I didn’t have family to take care of at that time.

So it’s really like a lot of privileges came together that allowed me to even fail that much.

And that’s also something we need to think about. Who gets to fail? And then who gets to talk about failure.

I always had this kind of secret plan B, which was to open a cinema.

And I think a lot of my friends in science, if you ask them, they always have like a secret plan B. And it’s usually to do with doing something lovely like opening a bakery or opening a bike shop.

And for me it was opening a cinema, a small indie cinema.

I don’t know if I would have done it actually if I left science. But it was kind of a nice fantasy to escape to, and it sometimes still is.

But I still think, "Oh, I can open a cinema if if everything else fails."

But I would not think of it as a failure.

Because I think there’s a lot of ways to leave science, or to leave academia, and do really interesting and really cool things.

So a lot of my friends who were at university with me are not practicing scientists anymore. Or at least not research scientists, but they do really cool things in industry, in education, in all kinds of sectors.

So this view of leaving science as a failure, I think, is quite problematic as well.

I think it’s really important to share failures as well, in order to distinguish what is a personal failure and what is a system failing you.

And if I submit a grant application and I don’t get the grant, that’s fine.

That might be that my idea wasn’t good enough. Or the grant wasn’t well enough thought out.

But if 100 of my friends submit grant applications and then only 10 of them, only five of them, get a grant, then that maybe points to there being not enough money for research or not enough funding.

And I think we need to open up about failures as well to see where there are places in the system where the system actually could be improved.

articles.personality_title: Scientists encourage sharing failures to support early-career researchers
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Science often involves many setbacks, especially for new researchers. Experiments can fail, funding can be hard to get, and not everyone succeeds right away. This can make young scientists feel alone and discouraged.

**What happened** – Professor Melanie Stefan, a scientist at Berlin Medical School, shared her own story of struggling with failure early in her career. After facing many rejections for funding and feeling isolated, she wrote an article suggesting scientists should openly share their failures in a 'CV of failures.' This idea was discussed at the Failure in Science conference at Imperial College London, where researchers talked about how failure is a normal part of science.

**Impact** – Stefan’s idea helps young scientists see that failure is common, not a sign they are alone or not good enough. By sharing failures, experienced scientists create a safer and more honest research environment. This can reduce stress and encourage learning from mistakes, similar to how engineers test and improve their work through trial and error.

**What's next step** – The scientific community is starting to accept failure as part of progress and is working to create spaces where researchers can safely try, fail, and try again. This may lead to changes in how science is taught and funded, making it more supportive for everyone, especially those just starting their careers.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Sharing stories of failure helps scientists learn, grow, and support each other in the challenging journey of research.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les scientifiques encouragent le partage des échecs pour soutenir les jeunes chercheurs
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La science implique souvent de nombreux échecs, surtout pour les chercheurs débutants. Les expériences peuvent échouer, il est difficile d’obtenir des financements, et tout le monde ne réussit pas immédiatement. Cela peut rendre les jeunes scientifiques isolés et découragés.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – La professeure Melanie Stefan, scientifique à l’École de médecine de Berlin, a partagé son propre parcours marqué par des échecs en début de carrière. Après de nombreuses refus de financements et un sentiment d’isolement, elle a écrit un article proposant que les scientifiques partagent ouvertement leurs échecs dans un « CV des échecs ». Cette idée a été discutée lors de la conférence Failure in Science à l’Imperial College de Londres, où les chercheurs ont parlé du fait que l’échec est une partie normale de la science.

**Impact** – L’idée de Stefan aide les jeunes chercheurs à comprendre que l’échec est courant, et non un signe d’incompétence ou de solitude. En partageant leurs échecs, les scientifiques expérimentés créent un environnement de recherche plus sûr et plus honnête. Cela peut réduire le stress et encourager l’apprentissage des erreurs, comme en ingénierie où l’on teste et améliore grâce aux essais et erreurs.

**Prochaine étape** – La communauté scientifique commence à accepter l’échec comme partie intégrante du progrès et travaille à créer des espaces où les chercheurs peuvent essayer, échouer et recommencer en toute sécurité. Cela pourrait changer la manière d’enseigner et de financer la science, la rendant plus accessible à tous, surtout aux débutants.

**En une phrase** – Partager les échecs aide les scientifiques à apprendre, grandir et se soutenir mutuellement dans le parcours difficile de la recherche.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos fomentan compartir fracasos para apoyar a investigadores jóvenes
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La ciencia a menudo implica muchos fracasos, especialmente para los investigadores que recién empiezan. Los experimentos pueden fallar, conseguir financiación es difícil y no todos tienen éxito de inmediato. Esto puede hacer que los jóvenes científicos se sientan solos y desanimados.

**Qué pasó** – La profesora Melanie Stefan, científica en la Escuela de Medicina de Berlín, compartió su propia experiencia con fracasos al inicio de su carrera. Tras enfrentar muchos rechazos para obtener fondos y sentirse aislada, escribió un artículo proponiendo que los científicos compartan abiertamente sus fracasos en un 'CV de fracasos'. Esta idea se discutió en la conferencia Failure in Science en el Imperial College de Londres, donde investigadores hablaron sobre cómo el fracaso es parte normal de la ciencia.

**Impacto** – La idea de Stefan ayuda a los jóvenes científicos a ver que el fracaso es común y no significa que estén solos o sean incapaces. Al compartir sus fracasos, los científicos experimentados crean un ambiente de investigación más seguro y honesto. Esto puede reducir el estrés y fomentar el aprendizaje de los errores, parecido a cómo los ingenieros prueban y mejoran sus diseños mediante ensayo y error.

**Próximo paso** – La comunidad científica está empezando a aceptar el fracaso como parte del progreso y trabaja para crear espacios donde los investigadores puedan intentar, fracasar y volver a intentar con seguridad. Esto podría llevar a cambios en la enseñanza y financiación de la ciencia, haciéndola más accesible para todos, especialmente para quienes comienzan.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Compartir historias de fracasos ayuda a los científicos a aprender, crecer y apoyarse mutuamente en el desafiante camino de la investigación.

articles.title: Volunteers from Poland remember how Poles opened their homes to Ukrainian refugees in 2022
articles.summary: Five years into the full-scale war, however, the border has also revealed the limits of that extraordinary solidarity.
articles.content:
Marcin Piotrowski remembers the beginning of his work in Ukraine through the Budomierz-Hruszów border crossing in February 2022, days after the launch of Russia’s war on Ukraine. “We crossed the border on the second day after the full-scale invasion,” he says, “and there were hundreds of people there. Nobody was helping them.”

People were waiting for days to enter Poland, some in cars and some on foot, as temperatures fell to around minus 15 degrees Celsius. On the Polish side, food and transport had been organised, but the queues on the Ukrainian side had become a challenge of their own. Piotrowski and volunteers from his Polish association, Folkowisko, decided to intervene. “We had experience because our association organises festivals,” he explains. “We put up tents, brought volunteers, and our medical service from the festival came as well. Later, we started helping at other border crossings, then in Lviv at the railway station, and we began working with volunteers from different parts of Ukraine.”

What began as emergency assistance developed into a network of projects across the Polish-Ukrainian border. Folkowisko helped establish a medical clinic and education centre in Nakhachiv, near the Polish border, where Polish and Ukrainian cultural workers have held joint workshops. The organisation has also supported psychological care, trained Ukrainian psychologists and social workers, and brought Ukrainian families affected by the war to Poland for temporary respite.

But Folkowisko's work is not only about the present. Piotrowski is also interested in the history of the border region, and in what happens when difficult memories are discussed through contact rather than isolation. “Before the Second World War, there were more than a thousand Ukrainians in the village where we work,” he says, referring to a locality in what is now eastern Poland. “Today, there are 43 people and they are all Polish. People were resettled in 1945 and 1947, during Operation Vistula. This was a place where Jews, Poles and Ukrainians lived together, and 80 years ago you could not really say where the border was.”

The history separating the two societies is particularly painful. During World War II, tens of thousands of Polish civilians were killed by Ukrainian nationalist formations in the Volhynia region. Polish nationalist groups retaliated, killing thousands of Ukrainian civilians. The competing memories of these events have remained politically sensitive, especially in families whose relatives were victims.

After the fall of communism, the history of Volhynia became increasingly prominent in Polish public debate. In Ukraine, meanwhile, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) acquired an important place in national memory because of its role in the struggle for Ukrainian independence against Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union. Disputes over monuments, commemorations, exhumations and historical figures have repeatedly affected relations between Warsaw and Kyiv.

The subject is also vulnerable to manipulation, according to Łukasz Wojtkowski, an assistant professor at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, who researches information operations and disinformation. He argues that historical grievances can be connected to contemporary fears and used to deepen divisions: “Volhynia is a playbook for propaganda and disguised disinformation,” he explains. “It is basically the only open case between those two nations that can spark the engine of disinformation and hatred. Russia can put two irons in the fire at the same time: it can increase the hatred between Poland and Ukraine, and it can reinforce the Russian narrative that there is a fascist regime in Kyiv.”

Anna Mierzyńska, a Polish journalist and social media researcher specialising in disinformation, has studied similar narratives targeting Polish audiences. “Reliable historical debate,” she stresses, “is always based on listening to both sides and taking new developments into account. Its purpose is not to attack or create hatred, but to explain what happened and find an understanding.” While there is such a debate among historians and experts, she adds that in the Polish information sphere, “many of the posts on this subject are designed to provoke hatred toward Ukrainians.”

Recurring narratives portray Ukrainians as a physical threat to Poles, Mierzyńska continues, using descriptions of the Volhynia crimes to create fear, or to suggest that Ukrainians could seek Polish territory. Existing social problems can also be folded into the same narrative. Long waiting lists for healthcare, for example, existed before the arrival of millions of Ukrainian refugees, but online claims blamed Ukrainians for them. Housing, employment and public services have been framed in similar ways.

The scale of Ukrainian displacement makes the relationship especially important. In 2026, nearly a million Ukrainians took temporary protection in Poland, representing 21.8 percent of all people from Ukraine under temporary protection in the European Union.

We need good contacts between Poles and Ukrainians, integration, getting to know each other and building trust. When we know each other well and trust each other, outside influence becomes much less important. – Anna Mierzyńska

For Piotrowski, the first months after the invasion demonstrated what such contact can look like. “Ordinary citizens living on the border with Ukraine were the first ones to provide immediate support,” he recalls. “I have never seen so much kindness in my life on both sides of the border, and so much reconciliation and understanding.”

Five years into the full-scale war, however, the border has also revealed the limits of that extraordinary solidarity. “I understand that when Poles opened their homes, it could become difficult,” Piotrowski says. “Someone comes who speaks another language, has slightly different customs and wants to stay for a long time. This is what I call empathy burnout.”

He does not regard that exhaustion as proof that the solidarity of 2022 was false, but rather, as a relationship being tested by time. His response is the same one that drives Folkowisko’s cultural work: more contact. “Poles don't know Ukrainians, Ukrainians don't know Poles,” he says. “Our job is to make people meet each other and understand each other.”

This approach means bringing difficult history into conversations in much the same way that Folkowisko’s festivals and programmes bring Polish and Ukrainian participants together while addressing the violence and displacement that transformed the region.

Wojtkowski is more cautious about whether historical reconciliation alone could resolve the wider conflict over competing narratives. “Imagine that tomorrow Poland and Ukraine commemorate every victim, Ukraine admits who was killed and how many people died, Poland admits what happened on its side, and all the exhumations are completed,” he posits. “It would not change everything, because Russia has other narratives.”

He maintains that, when it comes to history, both Polish and Ukrainian society did not do their homework properly. “In Poland, we learned the story of the interwar period as the restoration of the Polish state after more than a hundred years without independence,” he says, “but we did not always learn enough about the Ukrainian experience within that state. Ukraine has its own work to do in confronting everything that happened during the Second World War.”

Wojtkowski further advises that both Poland and Ukraine “should step very carefully, as if on very thin ice.” According to him, there should be signs of goodwill and a willingness to cooperate, but there is still a lot to do politically, academically and socially.

For Piotrowski, however, governments and historians do not have to resolve everything before ordinary people can build relationships: “We are trying to connect people who live ten or 15 kilometres from each other. They have different memories, different histories, but they can still meet and work together.”

As Ukraine moves toward the European Union, and as Polish and Ukrainian lives become increasingly intertwined, those everyday relationships may shape how the two societies handle their shared past. “If we lose the contact between ordinary people across both countries,” Piotrowski maintains, “then it becomes much easier to build the walls. And once the walls are there, it is much harder to build the bridges again.”

You can listen to an audio version of this story here.

This article was produced as part of the Thematic Networks of PULSE , a European initiative that supports transnational journalistic collaborations.

Anna Romandash is an award-winning journalist and co-author of “Women of Ukraine: Reportages from the War and Beyond.”

Nata Yasevych is a multimedia producer, media maker, and journalist, covering social issues and politics.

articles.personality_title: Polish volunteers build bridges for Ukrainian refugees despite historical challenges
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In 2022, after Russia launched a full-scale war on Ukraine, many Ukrainians fled to Poland seeking safety. This sudden arrival tested the kindness and limits of Polish communities near the border.

**What happened** – Polish volunteers, including Marcin Piotrowski and his group Folkowisko, quickly stepped in to help. They set up tents, provided medical care, and organized food and transport for refugees waiting in freezing conditions. Over time, their work grew into projects supporting education, psychological care, and cultural workshops for Ukrainians near the border.

**Impact** – This effort showed how people can come together to support each other even when facing language, cultural differences, and a difficult shared history. Folkowisko’s work also encourages Poles and Ukrainians to meet and understand each other, helping to reduce fear and misinformation that can cause division.

**What's next step** – Volunteers plan to continue bringing people together through cultural events and conversations about their shared past. Experts say this contact can help build trust and reduce hate, even if political and historical challenges remain. The goal is to keep connections strong so walls of fear do not grow.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Polish volunteers’ ongoing support and efforts to promote understanding offer a hopeful path for peaceful relationships between Poles and Ukrainians amid a difficult history and war.
articles.personality_title_fr: Des bénévoles polonais construisent des ponts pour les réfugiés ukrainiens malgré un passé difficile
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En 2022, après le lancement d’une guerre à grande échelle par la Russie contre l’Ukraine, de nombreux Ukrainiens ont fui vers la Pologne à la recherche de sécurité. Cette arrivée soudaine a mis à l’épreuve la solidarité des communautés polonaises proches de la frontière.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des bénévoles polonais, dont Marcin Piotrowski et son groupe Folkowisko, sont rapidement intervenus pour aider. Ils ont installé des tentes, fourni des soins médicaux et organisé la nourriture et le transport pour les réfugiés qui attendaient dans le froid glacial. Avec le temps, leur travail s’est étendu à des projets soutenant l’éducation, les soins psychologiques et des ateliers culturels pour les Ukrainiens près de la frontière.

**Impact** – Cet effort a montré comment des personnes peuvent s’unir pour s’entraider malgré les différences de langue, de culture et une histoire commune difficile. Le travail de Folkowisko encourage aussi Polonais et Ukrainiens à se rencontrer et à mieux se comprendre, aidant à réduire la peur et la désinformation qui peuvent diviser.

**Prochaine étape** – Les bénévoles prévoient de continuer à rassembler les gens à travers des événements culturels et des discussions sur leur passé commun. Les experts disent que ce contact peut aider à construire la confiance et réduire la haine, même si les défis politiques et historiques restent présents. L’objectif est de maintenir des liens forts pour éviter que les murs de la peur ne se construisent.

**Une phrase clé** – Le soutien continu des bénévoles polonais et leurs efforts pour promouvoir la compréhension offrent une voie d’espoir pour des relations pacifiques entre Polonais et Ukrainiens malgré une histoire difficile et la guerre.
articles.personality_title_es: Voluntarios polacos construyen puentes para refugiados ucranianos a pesar de un pasado difícil
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En 2022, tras el inicio de una guerra a gran escala por parte de Rusia contra Ucrania, muchos ucranianos huyeron a Polonia en busca de seguridad. Esta llegada repentina puso a prueba la solidaridad de las comunidades polacas cercanas a la frontera.

**Qué pasó** – Voluntarios polacos, incluyendo a Marcin Piotrowski y su grupo Folkowisko, actuaron rápidamente para ayudar. Montaron tiendas, ofrecieron atención médica y organizaron comida y transporte para los refugiados que esperaban en condiciones muy frías. Con el tiempo, su trabajo creció hacia proyectos que apoyan la educación, el cuidado psicológico y talleres culturales para ucranianos cerca de la frontera.

**Impacto** – Este esfuerzo mostró cómo las personas pueden unirse para apoyarse mutuamente a pesar de las diferencias de idioma, cultura y una historia compartida difícil. El trabajo de Folkowisko también promueve que polacos y ucranianos se conozcan y comprendan mejor, ayudando a reducir el miedo y la desinformación que pueden dividir.

**Próximo paso** – Los voluntarios planean seguir reuniendo a la gente mediante eventos culturales y conversaciones sobre su pasado común. Los expertos dicen que este contacto puede ayudar a construir confianza y reducir el odio, aunque sigan existiendo desafíos políticos e históricos. La meta es mantener fuertes las conexiones para evitar que crezcan muros de miedo.

**Una frase clave** – El apoyo continuo de los voluntarios polacos y sus esfuerzos por fomentar la comprensión ofrecen un camino esperanzador para relaciones pacíficas entre polacos y ucranianos en medio de una historia difícil y la guerra.
